title: ‘The State of Us’: Samuel Bottomley Breaks Callum Scott Howells Out of Hospice for One Final Hurrah in Edinburgh-Bound Indie (Exclusive Clip)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 11, 2026 3:00am Callum Scott Howells and Samuel Bottomley lead 'The State of Us' Courtesy of EIFF The Hollywood Reporter can unveil an exclusive clip from Ollie Gardner and Jake Harvey’s The State of Us , ahead of its premiere in competition at Edinburgh International Film Festival on Friday. Led by California Schemin ‘s Samuel Bottomley and It’s a Sin breakout star Callum Scott Howells , the British indie follows a boisterous tearaway called Frankie (Bottomley), who is struggling to come to terms with the inevitability of losing his best friend Taylor (Howells) to cancer. Frankie impulsively breaks Taylor out of hospice care for one final night of fun and debauchery, but what promises to be a night of hedonism quickly becomes something much more complicated. Related Stories Business RTL Boss Clement Schwebig on the Hybrid Future of European TV: "Scale Is Essential" Movies 'Congo Boy' Is an Autobiographical and Musical Refugee Drama. Its Director Has More in the Works. In the clip, Bottomley’s character can be seen cajoling Howells’ Taylor into having a drink and letting loose at a house party. On the dance floor, Taylor feels some semblance of relief as he reconnects with his childhood best friend. The characters in The State of Us are loosely based on Harvey’s childhood friendship group, in particular a friend called Jake Andrews, who died from cancer at the age of 18. Harvey and Gardner first met at university before pursuing careers in the arts — Harvey in TV, Gardner in theater — and with this movie, make their feature-length debuts. Co-starring with Bottomley and Howells are Frances Barber, Safia Oakley-Green, Seamus O’Hara, and Duggal Ram. Gardner told THR ahead of the film’s premiere: “I think it’d be quite nice for young men to see this film and see themselves in it from a perspective of, ‘Oh I can joke around and I know where the line is, but I also can really tap into the love that I feel for those male friendships.’ This is one very small seed that we’re trying to [plant] in the discourse of masculinity. We really want to dig into it because it’s such an incredibly complex and complicated theme.” Harvey added that he also hopes the humor lifts audiences heading to watch the film in the Scottish capital. “I think there’s a version of our film which was probably a bit more arthouse, a bit more serious, and more lends itself to that contemporary British type of independent cinema. But actually, [we’re] trying to do something that feels accessible,” he said. “It’s got its jokes and it’s dark humor, [and we hope] that it could actually reach the audience that it needs to speak to.” The 2026 Edinburgh International Film Festival runs from Aug. 14-21, and kicks off on Thursday with Louis Paxton’s The Incomer . Festival director Paul Ridd told THR he thinks it’s their greatest competition slate since they rebooted the event three years ago. “I’ve been very proud of everything we’ve done in 2024 [and] 2025… But this one, I think, is really kind of surpassing expectations.” Take a look at Samuel Bottomley and Callum Scott Howells in a clip from The State of Us below. title: George MacKay, Louisa Harland, Nathalie Emmanuel and Eric Kofi Abrefa Join ‘The Animals’ From ‘Supacell’ Star Calvin Demba (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 11, 2026 2:30am PT George MacKay, Louisa Harland, Nathalie Emmanuel and Eric Kofi Abrefa Join ‘The Animals’ From ‘Supacell’ Star Calvin Demba (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest George MacKay, Louisa Harland, Nathalie Emmanuel and Eric Kofi Abrefa Join ‘The Animals’ From ‘Supacell’ Star Calvin Demba (EXCLUSIVE) 11 minutes ago ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Fabien Frankel Joins Short Film ‘Love Unlimited’ (EXCLUSIVE) 43 minutes ago Pippa Harris and James Wilson to Headline London Film Festival Industry Forum 24 hours ago See All Photos supplied by filmmakers Calvin Demba, the British actor, writer and director best known on screen for the Netflix hit “Supacell,” has lined up an impressive cast list for his second short film behind the camera, “The Animals.” George MacKay (“Rose of Nevada,” “Sense and Sensibility”) stars alongside Louisa Harland (“Renegade Nell,” “Derry Girls”), Nathalie Emmanuel (“Game of Thrones,” “Megalopolis”) and Eric Kofi Abrefa (“Supacell,” BMF”) in the project, written and directed by Demba and produced by Tuli Litvak (“Beauty Sleep,” “Fairview Park”). Related Stories Dylan Mulvaney Fires Back After Trump Mocks Her and Kaitlan Collins in White House Correspondents' Dinner Speech: 'Actually the Greatest Compliment of All' CNN's Kaitlan Collins Was 'Not Surprised' Trump Insulted Her in White House Correspondents' Dinner Speech: 'That Happens Pretty Regularly Inside the Oval Office' “The Animals” centers on Miles (MacKay) as he struggles with growing feelings of emasculation and emotional impotency within his relationship with Remona (Harland). An opportunity to reclaim his sense of self arises from another man’s act of heroism during a violent home invasion — but as events spiral out of control, he’s forced to confront the destructive masculine ideals driving him. Popular on Variety “I wanted to make a film that takes a satirical look at gender stereotypes and the role they play in relationships,” said Demba, who made his directorial debut with 2022’s “BabyDolls.” “‘The Animals’ examines masculinity and how it can become performative. It pokes fun at modern relationships and the ways we unconsciously perform gender roles within them, exploring the gap between who we are and who we feel we should be. Tonally, the film is darkly comic, but the violence never feels slapstick. It needed to feel grounded in reality because that threat of violence mirrors the conversations we’re having about masculinity itself.” Added MacKay: “What drew me to the project was the script and the opportunity to work with Calvin. I’m a huge fan of his previous work and wanted to be part of whatever he made next. Working with Cal, and his mix of detail and freedom, was my favourite part of the process. His generosity as a writer and director, and his willingness to share that process, was golden.” “The Animals,” which was shot earlier this year, was filmed on 16mm by Ebba Hult (whose work has screened at Cannes, Telluride, and LFF), edited by Mdhamiri Á Nkemi (“The Last Tree,” “Blue Story”), and graded by Canadian colourist Jodie Davison (“The Revenant,” “The Eternal Daughter”). It is executive produced by BAFTA-winners Mouktar Mohammed (“Supacell”) and Sheila Nortley (“Supacell,” “Stay Close”), Demba and Harland. “This film was a total joy to make because we had such a clever script and such an incredible team, and I loved getting to work alongside George who I have long admired,” said Harland. “The script is what drew me to this role, but I really believe in Calvin as a filmmaker. His stories are rooted in poetry, and I hope to continue working with him on every project he does, whether that’s in front of or behind the camera.” “The Animals” will begin its festival circuit at a BAFTA and Oscar qualifying major festival, to be announced soon. title: RTL Boss Clement Schwebig on the Hybrid Future of European TV: “Scale Is Essential”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All August 11, 2026 1:45am RTL Group CEO Clement Schwebig Boris-Breuer Get big or die trying has become the strategy of Europe’s traditional broadcasters. Merger mania is everywhere. Last month, Comcast‘s Sky signed a $2.13 billion (£1.6 billion) deal to acquire British commercial broadcast giant ITV . Last year, MediaForEurope (MFE), the TV group controlled by the Berlusconi family, took majority control of German commercial network ProSiebenSat.1, adding to its pan-European conglomerate that includes Mediaset, Italy’s largest broadcaster, and Spain’s top commercial network Telecinco. The reasoning behind this consolidation is simple. European TV companies, seeing a decline in traditional advertising and fierce competition from streaming companies and online video giants like YouTube, have realized scale matters. If they are not to be wiped out completely, legacy broadcasters need to shift their business online — to digital ad and streaming subscription models — while staying big enough to still be profitable. Related Stories Movies 'Congo Boy' Is an Autobiographical and Musical Refugee Drama. Its Director Has More in the Works. Business European Broadcast Giant RTL Group Bets on Streaming to Fuel Growth RTL Group , Europe’s largest television company, is also playing the merger game. In June, RTL, which owns production giant Fremantle and is itself a subsidiary of German media conglomerate Bertelsmann, closed its acquisition of Comcast’s German pay-TV operation Sky Deutschland, folding it into its RTL+ streaming service. The combined platform, with 12.4 million paid subscriptions, is now the third-largest streamer in German-speaking Europe, behind Netflix and Amazon Prime. In France, where RTL owns commercial channel M6, it is investing heavily in its streaming platform M6+. First-half 2026 figures at RTL, released Tuesday , show how quickly the company is pivoting to streaming. Revenue growth in the division, up 27.2 percent to $345 million (€299 million) made up for the fall off in RTL’s traditional TV business. The shift to streaming is “already far advanced,” says RTL Group CEO Clement Schwebig, “Streaming is no longer an investment story for RTL Group, it is a profitability story.” Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter , Schwebig outlined RTL’s strategy for survival in a transforming TV business — and why he believes consolidation, combined with a hybrid model of free TV, pay TV and streaming, is the only way European media companies can build the scale to compete with the global platforms. “The future is not linear versus streaming,” he says. “The future is exclusive, local content distributed across every platform where our audiences want to spend their time.” RTL is quickly transitioning its traditional free-to-air ad model to streaming. How rapid do you see this transition and what role do you see free-to-air playing in RTL’s business model in the future? The transformation is already far advanced. Streaming is no longer an investment story for RTL Group, it is a profitability story. Our streaming businesses will contribute around €100 million ($115 million) to our operating profit this year. This is a turning point in our operation after years of carefully investing in content and “tech infrastructure,” streaming is now a high-margin contributor and high-growth segment at the same time. Our strategy is to combine the strengths of free TV, pay TV and streaming, of advertising, subscription and distribution revenues into one powerful ecosystem with unmatchable reach. Following the acquisition of Sky Deutschland, we now have 12.4 paid subscriptions in the German-speaking region – this brings us in striking distance to Netflix and Amazon in this market. In June alone, our advertising sales house had a net reach of almost 69 million across all media, reaching 87 percent of all persons in Germany. Linear TV is and will remain the backbone to reach such mass audiences. What are the content implications of this shift – what will the focus of RTL’s acquisition and production spending be going forward? The future is not linear versus streaming. The future is exclusive, local content distributed across every platform where our audiences want to spend their time. That is exactly where RTL is positioned: no other European media company produces so much local content at scale as we do. We have something that very few companies have: brands that speak to our local audiences and create an emotional connection with them – some of them even every day. Think of our news or long-running daily drama such as Good Times, Bad Times . Investing in premium sports is key to strengthening our linear TV channels and gaining users for our streaming services. Just look at the football World Cup 2026: 94 percent of French people watched the competition on M6 or M6+, almost the entire population. A huge figure and powerful demonstration for the strength of our brands. In Germany, the Bundesliga and German Cup competition will continue to excite fans across Sky and [streaming platform] Wow – with some selected matches also broadcast on our flagship channel RTL. The proposed sale of TF1’s production division Studio TF1 has reignited speculation that TF1 could make another bid for M6. How would you view such a bid, and how core is the French network to RTL’s business? Groupe M6 is a highly valuable, strategic asset for RTL Group and one of the best-managed media companies in Europe. We have been one of the founders and a committed shareholder since the launch of M6 in 1987. The long-term success of the company is close to our hearts at RTL. As we said repeatedly over the past years: we continue to believe that consolidation is necessary if European media companies want to compete effectively with global technology and streaming platforms. And we remain convinced that market consolidation will also happen in France sooner or later. Otherwise, the global players will dominate the European markets. I am very confident that Groupe M6 will play a key role in any further consolidation in the French media industry. The management team has taken some big bets to gain audience shares, and they are working out well – most prominently Cyril Hanouna on W9 and the football World Cup this year with record ratings. M6 has the youngest audience among the major French channels, and this makes its programme brands very attractive for advertisers. It shows how successful the management transition to David Larramendy and his team has been. That being said, any significant consolidation move requires a change of the current French media law – and positive signals from the regulators. What is Fremantle’s M&A strategy – are ITV Studios and Studio TF1 (if put up for sale) potential targets? Fremantle’s M&A strategy is very clear. We are focused on IP-driven acquisitions of small and medium-sized production companies that strengthen our position in attractive genres and geographies. We see only limited scale returns for large mergers in the content production space. Large transactions among content producers are often complex and produce limited synergies. As a matter of principle, we do not comment on specific companies or market speculation. Fremantle is one of top three independent production companies worldwide. It combines scale, a highly diversified business model across genres, markets and customers with strong profitability, reaching its target of a 9 percent profit margin this year. With beloved, long-lasting IP such as Got Talent , Farmer Wants A Wife and Baywatch , Fremantle has a proven track record in creating long-term monetisation opportunities through distribution, local adaptations and digital platforms. We are also excited about pursuing new opportunities in adjacent businesses, for example with sports content and in the larger creator economy. THR

title: ‘The End of Oak Street’: First Reactions
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All August 11, 2026 1:39am (L-r) Ewan McGregor as Greg Platt and Anne Hathaway as Denise Platt in The End of Oak Street, A Warner Bros. Pictures release. Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures Logo text Warner Bros. held a series of press screenings for its high concept sci-fi survival feature The End of Oak Street in the last few days, and the early reaction on social media suggests the studio may, finally, have a film to get it out of its box office rut in 2026. The logline for The End of Oak Street reads, “After a mysterious cosmic event rips Oak Street from suburbia and transports their neighborhood to someplace unknown, the Platt family soon discovers that their very survival depends on them sticking together as they navigate their now unrecognizable surroundings.” Related Stories Movies J.J. Abrams on 'The End of Oak Street' Theories and Daughter Gracie's Acting Debut: "I Know How Hard She's Working" Movies Anne Hathaway on Her Jam-Packed Year of Movies and Upcoming Adaptation of Hit Novel 'Yesteryear' Anne Hathaway , Ewan McGregor , Maisy Stella and Christian Convery star as the Platt family. The cast also includes P. J. Byrne and Chris Coy. The film was written, directed and produced by David Robert Mitchell , the filmmaker behind the highly rated 2014 horror film It Follows and A24’s 2018 black comedy Under the Silver Lake . Notably, The End of Oak Street is produced by J.J. Abrams as well as Hannah Minghella, Jon Cohen, Matt Jackson and Tommy Harper. There has been some online chatter that The End of Oak Street is secretly connected to Abrams’ Cloverfield franchise. Alas, Abrams shot down the speculation “The only connection to our Cloverfield movies is that Ewan’s partner is Mary Elizabeth Winstead, who was the star of 10 Cloverfield Lane , who we were very lucky to get to work with and who I adore,” Abrams told The Hollywood Reporter . “So there was that, but other than that, people are just making connections that they happen to see.” Full reviews of The End of Oak Street are embargoed until Aug. 12, ahead of the film’s wide theatrical release on Aug. 14. For Warners, there’s an added pressure for The End of Oak Street to succeed at the box office. The studio had a stellar 2025, when Sinners , A Minecraft Movie , Superman , Final Destination Bloodlines , Weapons and One Battle After Another all made hay at the global box office —and in the case of Sinners and OBAA dominated the Oscars. However, Warners has struggled this year, with The Bride! , Mortal Kombat II and Supergirl all proving to be huge bombs at the box office, with only Wuthering Heights finding any success. title: Fremantle Revenues Slide But Earnings Shoot Up To $69.2M
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Fremantle Revenues Slide But Earnings Shoot Up To $69.2M L.A. Creator Sachin Kumar Launches Prema Creative Co. With Vertical Comedy Series About Indian-American Actor In Hollywood Sony LIV Confirms ‘Scam 2010’ Production Will Go Ahead Despite Legal Threat View All August 11, 2026 1:07am 'Kill Jackie' AMC+/Fremantle Kill Jackie producer Fremantle saw its half-yearly revenues slide nearly 8% due to drama and film production, but earnings still shot up to nearly $70M. In results released by parent RTL this morning, the London-based company posted revenues of €835M ($963M), down 7.7% on the €905M from the same period last year. RTL attributed the fall to “timing effects at Fremantle’s drama and film business,” with entertainment and documentaries “broadly stable.” Fremantle will see the dip reverse in the second half of 2026, RTL projected, and post “slightly higher” numbers that he previous year due to upcoming productions such as AMC+’s Kill Jackie and Fox’s Baywatch . Related Stories Executives E.W. Scripps CEO Briefs Wall Street On Major Layoffs, Touts AI "Revolution" In Local TV News News Starz Subscriber Levels Climbed In Q2 Despite Price Increase, CEO Jeff Hirsch Says However, Fremantle was one of two units that RTL attributed to a significant increase in earnings across the group. Adjusted EBITA was up from €39M to €60, with the margin widening sharply from 4.3% to 7.2%. This puts Fremantle on track to reach a target margin of 9% for the full year. Watch on Deadline The news comes less than two weeks after Deadline revealed Fremantle had hired Katie O’Connell Marsh to become CEO of its Global Scripted Hub. Her role will be include building out Fremantle’s drama and comedy slate, while improving the revenue take from productions. Days after her hire became public, the Baywatch reboot sold to Prime Video in numerous territories. Fremantle’s latest financials come after RTL implemented cost saving measures at the production house following a strategic review. Part of the move saw Fremantle exit fully-financing films, though it will remain as a co-producer on projects. RTL noted cost reduction plans will continue until 2030 by “optimisation of production costs, simplification of processes [and] reduction of technical costs – driven by AI.” RTL profits rise Overall, Luxembourg-based RTL posted group revenues up 0.1% at €2.9B, with adjusted EBITA coming in at €239M, significantly higher than the €160M delivered in H1 2025. Excluding the impact of buying Sky for €68M, RTL posted group adjusted EBITA up €18M. Streaming revenue, which comes from services such as RTL+ and M6+, was up 27.2% to €299M, with the number of subscribers growing alongside higher pricing in Germany and “rapidly growing” ad money in Germany and France. In total, paid subscriptions for Germany and France – RTL’s biggest two territories – were up 20.7% to 8.7 million. Adjusted EBITA from streaming was €31M and is expected to reach around €100M for the full year, way up on previous guidance to analysts of around €25M-€50M. The result were also the first since RTL on June 1 completed a deal for Sky Deutschland , which posted adjusted EBITA of €61M in H1. RTL noted this would not be indicative of the whole year as June has no production costs attached to the Bundesliga or German Cup football. Once RTL+ and Sky Deutschland merge operations, RTL will have more than 12 million paying subs across in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. “RTL Group delivered a strong first half performance in 2026, driven by rapid streaming growth, gains in both TV audience and TV advertising market shares, and the successful completion of the acquisition of Sky Deutschland,” said RTL CEO Clément Schwebig. “We also demonstrated the unique power of our content and brands, as the coverage of the football World Cup on M6 and M6+ attracted 60 million viewers and generated exceptional digital engagement. “Our streaming businesses deliver strong profitability. Streaming revenue and paid subscriptions continue to grow dynamically. As a result, streaming is now expected to contribute around €100M to our full-year operating profit.” Schwebig, the former Warner Bros. Discovery exec, replaced Thomas Rabe as CEO earlier this year. Rabe remains boss of RTL parent Bertelsmann until later in the year. title: Hong Kong Filmmaker Ann Hui To Receive Camellia Award At Busan International Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Biggest Hollywood Film Of All Time In India; As First Half Box Office Show Signs Of Market Recovery ReelShort On Course To Reach $1BN Revenue & First Profit In 2026 – MPA Report Michelle Yeoh Named As Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Filmmaker Of The Year View All August 11, 2026 12:40am Ann Hui Busan International Film Festival This year’s Busan International Film Festival has named Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui as the recipient of the Camellia Award, presented to filmmakers who have made significant contributions to elevating the status of women in the film industry. Hui was a leading figure in the Hong Kong New Wave as a director, screenwriter and producer, making her directing debut with The Secret in 1979. She has continued making films consistently since then, building a body of work that includes 27 feature films and two feature-length documentaries, including multiple award winner A Simple Life , which won Best Actress at the Venice film festival for Deanie Ip’s performance in 2011. Related Stories News Michelle Yeoh Named As Busan International Film Festival's Asian Filmmaker Of The Year News Mouly Surya, Reza Rahadian & Prasanna Vithanage Among Filmmakers Selected For Busan's Asian Project Market Along the way, she has also won Best Director at the Hong Kong Film Awards six times and Best Director at the Golden Horse Awards three times. Both A Simple Life and Summer Snow (1995) achieved the rare feat of sweeping Best Film, Best Director, Best Actor, and Best Actress at the Hong Kong Film Awards. Watch on Deadline Hui has also been presented with Lifetime Achievement Awards at the 2012 Asian Film Awards, Asian Filmmaker of the Year Award at Busan film festival in 2014, and the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the 2020 Venice film festival. “Underlying Hui’s remarkable career and international acclaim is a singular cinematic vision rooted in compassion and humanity, one that has long captured the complexities of Hong Kong society and the spirit of its times,” said Busan film festival in a statement. “Spanning a wide range of genres, her films chronicle the everyday lives of ordinary people while weaving intimate personal stories into broader social realities. Her nuanced portrayals of women, particularly those often pushed to the margins, have resonated deeply with audiences across cultures and generations.” Hui commented on the award: “In my previous years I felt unwilling to receive such taking-stock prizes because I wished to continue making movies. Now that I’m nearly eighty and find it difficult to make a film, I think the prize comes just in time for me to appreciate it more.” She added, “I am so happy to return to Busan and meet an audience that is among the most savvy and cinematically literate in the world.” Busan partnered with Chanel to establish the award, named after Gabrielle Chanel’s favorite flower, which was last year awarded to Taiwanese actress, director and producer Sylvia Chang. This year’s Camellia Award will be presented at Busan’s opening ceremony on October 6. As previously announced, the festival has also named Michelle Yeoh as this year’s Asian Filmmaker of the Year. title: ‘Pacifiction’ Director Albert Serra on His New Film ‘Sixteen Moments of My Life’ and Why He’d Love to Have Directed Elvis Presley
full_text: Aug 11, 2026 12:09am PT ‘Pacifiction’ Director Albert Serra on His New Film ‘Sixteen Moments of My Life’ and Why He’d Love to Have Directed Elvis Presley ‘I want to do a ‘Brigadoon’-style musical comedy,’ Serra tells Variety at Locarno, where ’16 Moments of My Life’ world premieres By John Bleasdale Plus Icon John Bleasdale Guest Contributor Latest Heritage Monday at the Locarno Film Festival Sees a Future in the Past 4 hours ago Zoe Saldaña on Seeing ‘Terminator’ Aged 7, Having the Wrong-Shaped Feet and Wanting to Direct: ‘Give Me That Camera!’ 20 hours ago Protest at the Locarno Film Festival Remembers 60,000 Names of the Dead of Gaza 2 days ago See All Ingrid Caven in Sixteen Moments of My Life. Courtesy of the Locarno Film Festival Don’t call Albert Serra ’s new film, “Seize moments de ma vie” (“ Sixteen Moments of My Life ”), a concert film. Premiering out of competition at the Locarno Film Festival , the film documents a one-off performance by screen legend Ingrid Caven at the Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord in Paris. “I will never shoot a concert unless I’m involved in the music,” Serra told Variety . The band were Molforts, the Catalan musicians who provide Serra’s soundtracks and Caven has been friends with the Spanish director for over fifteen years. Famed for her performances in the sixties and seventies of many European film classics as well as being the muse and frequent collaborator of her sometime husband, Rainer Werner Fassbinder, Caven is also a recording artist and Serra requested that they collaborate together with the musicians writing the music sending it over on CDs and Caven improvising over the music. Related Stories CNN's Kaitlan Collins Was 'Not Surprised' Trump Insulted Her in White House Correspondents' Dinner Speech: 'That Happens Pretty Regularly Inside the Oval Office' Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread “Over the years the musicians and Caven wrote 16 songs, going back and forth. All this process, but they didn’t communicate directly. This is the point. They only communicate through the music itself. They didn’t talk.” Popular on Variety Not so much the director as the MC? “I had all these things in front of me, I could hardly see the stage.” This is how Serra also directs his films, such as “Liberté” and “Pacifiction.” “Everything is based on non-communication with the actors. I like when things happen without really working on meanings or on the outcome. Subconscious. Like old school Hollywood, you know, everybody has to do what they have to do, and we don’t need to discuss for hours. This was a similar concept.” The film continues Serra’s interest in performance. His last film, the documentary “Afternoons of Solitutde,” took as its subject a young and celebrated bullfighter and focused intently on him to the exclusion of everything else. So in “Sixteen Moments,” there are no cut-aways to the audience. “You have genius musicians on stage, and you want me to shoot some idiots watching them? No,” says Serra. The music is a mixture of autobiography sung in a way that drifts between opera, cabaret and Edith Piaff. At the very beginning we see Caven coughing before taking the stage. “Every performance is kind of life and death, and it’s unique: it’s fatality. Cinema is perfect for that, because cinema has the same logic. One moment of the film has passed, you cannot grab it, it’s passed. The experience of cinema, it’s the logic of live music or live performance. It has passed, and you cannot recover it. It’s very coherent with this fragility of creating musical life. You know that not everything is perfect. Not everything is under control always. And maybe this is part of the motion and the magic.” Having done a film on bullfighting and a singer, would there be another kind of performance he would like to document? “No, what would it be?” Serra says; then breaks into a grin. “I will do a musical comedy. This is something that has been a lot of times in my mind. I think I will end up doing it because I like this idea of musical comedy that’s positive. The spirit of something that is light: poetic and positive. Nowadays, with all this reality of the war and these problems and frictions and tensions and whatever, I’d like to make a “Brigadoon” style musical. Maximum happiness. The opposite of what I’ve been doing all of my life.” He also says that he wished he could’ve directed Maria Callas and Elvis Presley. “Elvis should have done dramatic roles, and with the right director, he would have been an amazing dramatic actor. And another idea I had was to make light comedies with Maria Callas, because she did only very very dramatic stuff with Pasolini. Very static like this opera and this intensity and this mythological stuff and very heavy. Why not make a comedy with her?” It might not be boasting. Serra’s films have featured some iconic performances, such as Jean-Pierre Léaud as Louis XIV in “The Death of Louis XIV” and Benoît Magimel in “Pacifiction.” Of the latter, Serra says: “It’s the best performance of his career. Whatever people say: no, this is the best performance. I know it. I’m 100% sure.” From Wednesday, Serra is back in the editing suite working on his new film “Out of This World” which he hopes to have completed by the end of the year. “It’s 65% done.” The film stars Riley Keough and F. Murray Abraham as part of an American delegation traveling to Russia in the context of the Ukraine war. “It’s not a war film, it’s about economics. You’ll see what happens in the film, where it goes at the end. It goes to the best scene of recent cinema. This I can tell you. So you will have to wait until the end.” That sounds like a headline. “Yes! And the second headline is ‘You will have to wait until the end.’” Albert Serra Copyright: Oscar Fernández Orengo ‘Sholay’ to Make ‘Films in Concert’ World Premiere at London’s Royal Albert Hall Sony’s Indian Version of ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?’ Hosted by Amitabh Bachchan, Adds Google Gemini as AI Guide (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: ‘Congo Boy’ Is an Autobiographical and Musical Refugee Drama. Its Director Has More in the Works.
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 11, 2026 12:01am 'Congo Boy' Courtesy of Trigon Film Robert is a 17-year-old Congolese refugee in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic (CAR). After his parents are imprisoned, he must care for his four younger siblings while striving to become a musician. That is the story of Congo Boy from director Rafiki Fariala. But it is also his, or at least inspired by his personal story. The landmark co-production by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the CAR, which world premiered in the Un Certain Regard competition of the Cannes Film Festival, where it won its star Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset the best actor honor in the session, is now unspooling on the big outdoor square in Switzerland, namely the Piazza Grande as part of the 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival , on Tuesday, Aug. 11. Related Stories Movies James Gray Rejects Men Not Being "Allowed to Engage With the Tender Side" Movies Keke Palmer, Deepa Mehta, Jacob Tremblay, and Jeremy Irons Projects Set for TIFF Financing Market Congo Boy ‘s cast is led by Dembeasset and also features Christy Djomanda Louba, Pétruche Mbomba, Rosiana Kotozia, Gloria Ambacko and Dieufera Sana. The screenplay was written by Fariala, Tommy Baron and Boris Lojkine. Adrien Lallau handled the cinematography, with editing by César Simonot. The autobiographical film – Fariala is the son of Congolese parents, based in the CAR and a self-taught musician – previously made the 2022 documentary We, Students! , in which he turned the camera on himself and his friends to capture everyday student life at Bangui University. Congo Boy is a production of Mahongo Films in the CAR, co-produced by Kiripifilms in the DRC, which is the company of filmmaker Dieudo Hamadi ( Kinshasa Makambo , Downstream to Kinshasa ), and France’s Unité. You may wonder just how autobiographical the movie is. “It is really my own story, told through Robert, played by Bradley,” Fariala told THR via a translator just before the film’s world premiere. “When you see in the film that Robert is shot at, I was actually shot at.” The same is true for Robert’s stay with a colonel and his participation in a talent show, co-organized by UNICEF, among other things. ‘Congo Boy’ Courtesy of Cannes Film Festival The filmmaker sees his experience as a refugee as something that reflects the lives of many people around the world and is showcased in the film. “My family fled the Congo because there was war there, and when we got to the Central African Republic, war started there, too,” Fariala explained. “They wanted to be in a country that was more at peace to protect their family. So they were thinking of going to Benin and then on to Europe to have some stability for our future. But unfortunately, they had passports and their refugee card that showed a different country, so they got arrested.” After We, Students! was censored in the CAR, he had to go into exile in France, again as a refugee. “We often speak about refugees who want to go to Europe, but there are a lot of people who are refugees within different countries of Africa,” as the film shows, said the director. “And I want to convey that refugees are not beggars. They have to leave their home because this world is really crazy because of human destruction. But the young ones still want to fight; they still have hopes and dreams. I am proud to be a refugee.” How did the director find his cast to tell a very personal story? “We did some street casting,” he recalled, highlighting that he added a French casting director to his Central African Republic crew to find the lead actor. “He’s my double,” emphasized Fariala. “It took months. I started looking into young singers on the music scene, but they lacked charisma. So I went to look for Congolese refugees, and we went to cultural centers in different neighborhoods. At this school at 6 a.m., we auditioned 50 young boys, including Bradley, and he was so different from the others. He was reserved and smiling, but he had something in common with me. He liked to sing and rap, but only in his bedroom, because his father didn’t want to hear anything about art. His father just wanted his son to do well in school, like mine. So I gave him an improv exercise about failing his high school degree, and it was very different from the others.” Fariala was convinced that the young man was the right person to play the lead role. “But I had to talk to his parents, who didn’t agree at first,” he shared with THR . “So I had to be very persuasive.” ‘Congo Boy’ Courtesy of ‘Congo Boy’ – Makongo Films/Unité/Kiripifilms/Karta Film/Canal+ The rest of the cast is also made up of non-professional actors. And many portray their real-life experience, such as soldiers appearing in the film as soldiers, and Fariala’s aunt playing herself. That plays into the filmmaker’s interest in both documentary and fiction, and in mixing the two in his films. “I started out in documentary, but I always like to add a layer of fiction into my documentaries,” he told THR . And Congo Boy is a fictionalized version of his own life, with the reliance on a non-professional cast adding another layer of documentary vibe, he noted. What’s next for Fariala? “For my next projects, whether they are documentary or fiction, I want to keep doing that,” mixing genres, the filmmaker told THR . “I have another documentary that I started filming before Congo Boy . It’s called To Live and is about one year of my life after We, Students! was released and was censored in the Central African Republic and I had to go into exile in France.” What awaits audiences? “I was a bit lost in France,” the creative shared. “I was lonely, and I didn’t know how to talk to people, how to interact, and so I felt homesick. And I filmed myself to live. The camera became my friend; it kept me busy. At the same time, my little sister was sending me footage of the family back home, which helped me really hang in there. So, this will be my next film.” But Fariala has more in the works. “I have written another fiction film which could be a sequel to Congo Boy , because of this character of Robert,” he told THR . “I want to see what happens when he has become a musician and when he becomes famous and how, when he’s accepted in the Central African Republic, he is going to live with success. I want to keep digging into that.” THR

title: ‘Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO’ Director Kamiyama Kenji Built His New Series Around a Metaphor for AI Fears: ‘Will We End Up Being Used by It?’
full_text: Aug 11, 2026 12:00am PT ‘Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO’ Director Kamiyama Kenji Built His New Series Around a Metaphor for AI Fears: ‘Will We End Up Being Used by It?’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO’ Director Kamiyama Kenji Built His New Series Around a Metaphor for AI Fears: ‘Will We End Up Being Used by It?’ 3 hours ago ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Battle Atop U.K., Ireland Box Office 3 hours ago Boxing Legend Chris John Joins Silver Media Group for Animated Series ‘Dragon’s Dojo’ (EXCLUSIVE) 9 hours ago See All ©SUNRISE Kamiyama Kenji says the alien threat driving his new “Gundam” anime is a direct metaphor for humanity’s uneasy relationship with artificial intelligence. The director, known for “Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex” and “The Lord of the Rings: The War of the Rohirrim,” tells Variety he built “ Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO ” around that anxiety. The series follows Ray Azumi (voiced by Takeo Otsuka), a war orphan who awakens on the lunar surface as the pilot of the experimental mobile suit Gundam ZERO. The story begins decades after humanity is forced to abandon Earth in the face of a hostile, self-replicating ecosystem born from an alien object’s three revelations: gravity control, faster-than-light communication and cognitive materialization. Humanity marks the years since in a calendar counted from that exile. Related Stories Singapore's First Wuxia Film 'The House on the Moon' Unveils Clip Ahead of Locarno Competition Bow: Director Nelson Yeo 'Decided to Fully Embrace Genre' (EXCLUSIVE) 'Donkey Princess' Review: A Princess Escapes the Kingdom, but Not the Patriarchy, in an Inventive, Shape-Shifting Fairytale Kamiyama explains why he placed Ray in a world where that exile is simply the everyday condition rather than a recent trauma: “As I explored, at the setting stage, the idea that this world too has a time ‘before today,’ I came to feel that rather than spelling out the setting from scratch, it would enrich the story more to let viewers imagine and fill in for themselves what came before today.” Popular on Variety The new setting hinges on those three revelations turning catastrophic. Asked what that premise let him explore, Kamiyama says: “Can we truly master a technology we did not create ourselves, or will we end up being used by it? It is a metaphor for technologies that humanity is already beginning to struggle to handle in reality, such as AI.” When it comes to moving between giant, established mythologies like “Gundam,” “Star Wars” and Tolkien’s Middle-earth, Kamiyama strives to put his own spin on things while also staying true to what the fans want. “I try to prepare surprises while taking the utmost care not to stray from that consensus,” he says. “When that goes well, the sense of sharing the moment with the fans becomes the motivation to keep creating — that’s what I believe.” “Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO” also encompasses the companion video game, “Gundam Rogue Orbit.” “The project actually started from the game first, but the game side had no fixed setting in place, so I built out the world starting from the question of what Gundam fights,” Kamiyama says. He left the game’s mechanics to its own team, reasoning that “games have an appeal that only a game can deliver, the fun that comes from the gameplay and the controls.” To prepare a backstory for “Gundam Rogue Orbit,” Kamiyama had to work out what the monsters were, what they did to Earth and humanity, and how long it took for either side of the coming war to develop a countermeasure like Gundam. “Creating these fine details is, I’d say, both the hardest part and the real thrill of building a science fiction work,” he says. On what keeps pulling him back to stories about societies adapting to systems they can’t control, Kamiyama believes that “anti-war is a universal theme; even as the forms and meanings of war change with the times, it remains timeless.” He extends that idea to the current moment: “The true nature of war looks different from one era to the next. Perhaps it is the unease of the wars unfolding right now.” Building an era untethered from Gundam’s Universal Century or 00 timelines gave him that freedom, he says. On his approach to legacy IP after working with Tolkien and Lucasfilm’s properties, he says, “It was about choosing between what should be carried on and what should be built anew.” Kamiyama also reveals the scale of the world he has built beyond what “RG XARX-ZERO” itself shows. “At the very least, it stretches from 50 years before the point where this story begins to the start of another possible future that could connect to the game’s world 100 years later,” he says. For the science-fiction concepts underpinning that world, including gravity control, faster-than-light communication and cognitive materialization, Kamiyama worked with novelist Toh EnJoe, credited as SF setting supervisor, as an outside arbiter. “He is a master who rearranges words through mathematics, so whether or not to examine meaning became a source of creative inspiration,” Kamiyama says, describing EnJoe’s rulings on which ideas were plausible, needed more thought, or could be glossed over. Asked what he hopes is the first surprise for viewers meeting this world, Kamiyama says: “Gundam’s place within a body of work that has always had giant robots as its protagonists.” The director has spent two decades moving between franchises with devoted fan bases, from his breakout run steering “Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex” through its two seasons, to co-directing Netflix’s CG reboots of “Ultraman” and “Ghost in the Shell: SAC_2045” with Shinji Aramaki. His theatrical foray into Middle-earth with “The Lord of the Rings: The War of the Rohirrim” reached screens worldwide in 2024, and he now oversees the “Star Wars: Visions” universe as supervising director on its 2026 installment, which extends the story he introduced in “The Ninth Jedi.” “Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO,” produced by Bandai Namco Filmworks with animation from Sola Animation, launches in 2027. ‘Sholay’ to Make ‘Films in Concert’ World Premiere at London’s Royal Albert Hall Sony’s Indian Version of ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?’ Hosted by Amitabh Bachchan, Adds Google Gemini as AI Guide (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: Locarno: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Piluk,’ From the National Film Board of Canada, Discuss the Language of Animation
full_text: Aug 10, 2026 11:55pm PT Locarno: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Piluk,’ From the National Film Board of Canada, Discuss the Language of Animation Following the journey of a girl called Piluk, born with wings, the film has its world premiere at Locarno's Pardi di Domani section By Kambole Campbell Plus Icon Kambole Campbell Latest Locarno: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Piluk,’ From the National Film Board of Canada, Discuss the Language of Animation 3 hours ago Marco Bellocchio, Sally Wainwright Win Big at Italian Global Series Festival Which Celebrated ‘Star Trek’ and ‘Lost’ and Lamented Industry Crisis 4 weeks ago ‘Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan’ Recalled by Director Nicholas Meyer 1 month ago See All 'Piluk' directors Elisapie Isaac and Marc Séguin Credit: Éva Maude With a world premiere in the Locarno Film Festival ‘s Pardi di Domani selection of short and medium-length films, the filmmakers behind “Piluk” saw the production as a chance to tell a story with the simplest possible textures: pencil, paper and the human voice. Produced by Marc Bertrand and Jelena Popović of the National Film Board of Canada and directed by multidisciplinary artists and longtime friends Marc Séguin and Elisapie Isaac, “Piluk” was created from over 8,000 drawings using pen, charcoal and pencil and accompanied by a soundtrack of throat-singing. Related Stories Aymar Esse, Director of Locarno Open Doors World Premiere ‘My Father’s Kora,' Explores the Challenges of Queer Identity in Senegal Odd Slice Films Boards Documentary ‘Concrete Land’ Ahead of Locarno Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Piluk’ Courtesy of the National Film Board of Canada “I have the most immense respect for things that can be said with pencil and paper,” Séguin says in an interview with Variety. “ Given all the technology that surrounds us, I still think that not all has been said with paper and pencil. So we wanted to go back to that craftsmanship. I mean, if Eli’s on stage or she records something for this film, it’s her voice. We didn’t want machines to be involved or ask AI to get involved as well, we wanted to just draw it the old-fashioned way.” Popular on Variety The story follows the journey of a girl called Piluk, born with wings on her back, as she crosses the countryside, eventually arriving at an unnamed city, caring for different animals along the way. There’s no dialogue: everything is communicated by its animation and by the expressive vocals of the choral soundtrack. The scratchy, sketchy linework goes for an impression of people and places rather than strictly realistic representation; the backgrounds mostly stripped away. Isaac says that the same principles applied to the soundtrack: the musician, being from an Inuk background, has spoken previously about taking inspiration from traditions of oral storytelling. Isaac says that at first she had been content to collaborate with Séguin in pre-production, but that “[when] it became clear that we’re not gonna overproduce, we’re not gonna over-add,” she began to want to experiment with the human voice. She enjoyed the sense of ambiguity to the way the voices mix with the imagery, that it feels organic this way, Isaac says. “We ended up keeping it very minimalist. What came out is just trying to respect what’s going on in the image and the world.” The idea of allowing room for audiences to project something of their own meaning was important for both the visuals and the soundtrack. “I think that was the purpose,” Isaac says of her approach to the music, “to leave space for people to feel.” To Isaac, lyrics and actual words or even “perfect melody” would be too structured; they wanted unpredictability. Courtesy of the National Film Board of Canada Though Séguin is renowned for his painting and has worked in filmmaking before (as has Isaac — the two have even collaborated before on projects such as Séguin’s 2016 feature “Stealing Alice”), producer Jelena Popović, who took over from Bertrand during the project, points out that both are new to animation as a medium. So it became part of NFB’s responsibility to support the artists in new territory, preserving their voice in the adaptation to working in a new format. This is, in Popović’s eyes, something inherent to NFB’s structure. “We are allies of the artist in a sense that we’re not profit driven, we’re a public money-funded producer and distributor,” she says. Making sure the artists can navigate this new space is but a small part of maintaining a sense of their influence over the story, something which extends to the NFB’s commitment to producing work by Indigenous artists. “The NFB obviously has a commitment to producing work by Indigenous storytellers and artists,” Popović says. “Many other indigenous artists work with the NFB, and hopefully we decolonize the institution through all of this work,” she adds, after listing works by artists such as Terril Calder, Jeff Barnaby and Walter Scott. “So in working with Elisapie and Marc, like any other filmmaker, and especially Indigenous filmmakers, it’s important to preserve this narrative sovereignty of the auteur. We are there to help! We are not there to prescribe anything nor impose anything.” The team of animators at the NFB studio was led by Parissa Mohit (“an amazing filmmaker and animator,” Popović says). “Parissa was their advisor for animation directing, and also the head of the animation team. These amazing exchanges, like the finessing of mise-en-scène and creating that illusion of movement, were really discussed in detail with Parissa and our technical director Eric Pouliot and the rest of our technical experts in-house.” Popović highlights the goal of supporting artists and helping them achieve their specific creative vision, describing NFB as a “creative laboratory.” “Artists come to us with an idea, and we give them a playground to explore in the development phase, and do many kinds of explorations [which] are really not easy to get in the private commercial sector,” Popović says. “We are not based on return on investment.” For Popović, who has also produced shorts such as “Hedgehog’s Home,” “Manivald” and “Bread Will Walk,” the film being made in the way the artists envisioned is the real return on investment — something which stems from a passion and belief in animation as “the sum and the summit of all arts with a capital A.” This is because, as Popović puts it, animation is “using the language of all the visual arts,” folding theater, drama and music into a cinematic language. “At the same time it’s an economical way of storytelling which is painstakingly long to make: you have to start from stereotypes and archetypes because that’s the language you know, and especially in short film animation, you have to adapt yourself to that economy of storytelling.” In their approach to “Piluk,” co-directors Séguin and Isaac have found just that kind of economy: finding the maximum emotional impact with the most minimal of art styles and musical instruments. title: Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities
full_text: Aug 10, 2026 11:37pm PT Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities The gathering is part of the Gramado Film Market and discusses the audiovisual industry’s role as a development driver By Marcelo Cajueiro Plus Icon Marcelo Cajueiro Latest Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities 3 hours ago Luiz Carlos Barreto, Brazil’s Legendary Film Producer, Dies at 98 3 weeks ago Brazil’s Gramado Fest Set to Honor ‘I’m Still Here’ Star Selton Mello and ‘The Secret Agent’ Standout Maria Fernanda Cândido 3 weeks ago See All Marcelo Pedrazzi, Maria Fernanda Galeano Rojo, Gabriel Portela and Letícia Friedrich, speakers at the Gramado Film Market. Courtesy Gramado Film Festival The First International Meeting of Cities will take place Aug. 12-14 at the Gramado Film Market and will gather municipal-level authorities from such major towns as Medellín, Rio de Janeiro, Porto Alegre, Maricá and fest-host Gramado as well as representatives of Brazilian and Ibero-American organizations to discuss how the creative economy — particularly the audiovisual industry — can contribute to social and economic development. The program will highlight the successful cases of the 2.4-million-strong city of Medellín, Colombia, and Gramado, a tourist town with 40,000 residents in Southern Brazil, said Ralfe Cardoso, general coordinator of the Gramado Film Market. Related Stories Dylan Mulvaney Fires Back After Trump Mocks Her and Kaitlan Collins in White House Correspondents' Dinner Speech: 'Actually the Greatest Compliment of All' Whitney Cummings' Donald Trump Sex Trafficking Joke Was Cut From Mark Twain Ceremony on Netflix; Streamer Says Kennedy Center Axed It Maria Fernanda Galeano Rojo , Medellín’s secretary of economic development, and Karla Valderrama, coordinator of the city’s film commission, will present in a panel the Colombian city’s experience in urban transformation — considered a model for other cities in Latin America — innovation, attracting audiovisual productions, and promoting economic and social development through the creative economy. Popular on Variety As for Gramado, Cardoso said the 54 consecutive annual editions of the film fest were a major driver turning the town into one of Brazil’s best-known tourist destinations. Gramado, in the mountains of Brazil’s southernmost state Rio Grande do Sul, offers European-inspired architecture, a strong gastronomic scene and several entertainment-themed complexes. “The growth of tourism in Gramado is connected to the film festival,” Cardoso told Variety . “It all began 54 years ago. Gramado today ranks as the country’s second tourism destination, behind only Rio de Janeiro. The film festival created that. It’s interesting, because it’s something that began with art.” The 10th edition of the Gramado Film Market will feature panels and pitching sessions, with the participation of execs from major companies such as Amazon MGM Studios, the Globo group’s Globo Filmes and streamer Globoplay , distributors Downtown Filmes, H2O Films and Vitrine Filmes , and Fernando Meirelles’ production company O2 Filmes . The Gramado Film Market’s forum will offer panels on key issues facing the local and international film and TV industries. Letícia Friedrich will present the panel Vitrine Filmes: Sponsorship, Investment, Circulation and Impact. Friedrich, a partner and director of Vitrine, will address how public policy, investment and distribution strategy can work together to strengthen indie cinema. Founded 15 years ago, Vitrine has built to become the leading distributor of Brazilian art features. The company distributed locally Kleber Mendonça’s “The Secret Agent,” which sold about 2.5 million admissions in the country, a spectacular performance for a Brazilian non-comedy art film. The panel’s theme is the company’s Vitrine Petrobras Session, a program sponsored by Brazil’s state-owned oil giant Petrobras. As part of the program, Vitrine has released more than 80 Brazilian films in sessions with affordable ticket prices and organized discussions, training activities and masterclasses in film societies, schools and cultural institutions. “Our project was created to democratize access to independent cinema by promoting Brazilian releases in commercial theaters across all regions of the country,” Friedrich told Variety . “Since 2023, the project has also invested in restoring and re-releasing classics of Brazilian cinema, reaffirming its commitment both to preserving the audiovisual memory and to promoting the country’s cinematic heritage.” Audiovisual public policy specialist Gabriel Portela will take part on the panel Future Perspectives for the Brazilian Audiovisual Industry. He will discuss the sector’s technological transformations, new consumption habits, changing financing models and distribution challenges. “The first question we need to address is developing strategies and policies so that Brazilian films can truly find its audience within the country. We cannot think about the development of our audiovisual industry without a strong domestic market,” Portela told Variety . Marcelo Pedrazzi, director and partner of Quanta, one of Brazil’s leading audiovisual infrastructure and services companies, will participate on the panel Innovations in the Audiovisual Process: Technology, Efficiency and New Production Workflows. He will provide a historical view of the technological evolution since the Lumière brothers’ first dedicated public screenings of moving images in 1895. “Over the past 25 years, the sector has undergone a major wave of transformation driven by innovation and technology. title: Linda Cardellini Reveals Homage To Betsy Palmer In ‘Crystal Lake’: “A Certain Sweater Makes An Appearance”
full_text: Skip to main content By Rosy Cordero Rosy Cordero Associate Editor, TV @SocialRosy More Stories By Rosy Linda Cardellini Reveals Homage To Betsy Palmer In ‘Crystal Lake’: “A Certain Sweater Makes An Appearance” ‘Sunset P.I.’ Bosses Dan Goor & Luke Del Tredici On Finding Inspiration From ‘Moonlighting’ & ‘The Pitt’ ‘Line Of Fire’s Josh Safran & Peter Krause Tease New NBC Series View All August 10, 2026 11:30pm Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees in 'Crystal Lake' Peacock The new Peacock series Crystal Lake will welcome a new scream queen in Linda Cardellini , who will play the role of Pamela Voorhees, mother of Jason Voorhees, the infamous serial killer from the F riday the 13th films. Ahead of the streaming series’ premiere on Thursday, October 15, Cardellini and Brad Caleb Kane, writer, showrunner, and executive producer of the series, hosted a panel on Monday afternoon at the NBC Backlot Press Day. “We all know where Pam ends up because she starts all the killing in the first movie. So, what Brad gave me was a beautiful beginning and somewhere to go. There’s an arc there from somebody who means well and is trying to survive. She’s doing the best that she can and fighting hard for things that she thinks are right to [becoming] somebody who then turns out to do all the wrong things. That gives me a lot of places to go. I think that dissent is very necessary,” Cardellini shared. Related Stories News Peacock Launches First Serialized Mobile Game 'Public Eye' News 'Love Island USA' Cements Its Crown As Peacock's Top Original Series The role of Pam has been played by multiple actresses, but the gold standard is Betsy Palmer, the first to play the serial killer mom of a serial killer, in the 1980 film Friday the 13th . Since news of the prequel series broke, there have been questions about how Cardellini will approach playing the character. Watch on Deadline NBCUNIVERSAL EVENTS — “Backlot Pass Day” — Pictured: (l-r) Linda Cardellini, Brad Caleb Kane, Showrunner, Executive Producer at the Universal Studios Lot on Monday, August 10, 2026 “I have, of course, seen what Betsy Palmer did. Then you see a little bit more of it in [ Friday the 13th Part 2]; she kind of comes back as the severed head. The fans love her so much. We even toyed around with the idea of the short hair, but we figured she has 10 years to get there,” she said. Adding, “You can’t duplicate what Betsy did, which was to play this devoted mother. So I can take that and sort of bring that to the early childhood years of Jason’s life. I also think that you don’t get to where Betsy is without really truly loving Jason and getting to know him. That was really important to us going in. And no, you can’t be another Betsy. But I do do a little bit of an homage with a certain sweater that makes an appearance.” The famous sweater Cardellini is referring to is the one worn by Palmer in the original film when Pam was decapitated by a camp counselor. Without giving too much away about the pilot episode, there’s a scene where Cardellini ends up with about a bucket’s worth of blood all over her. Trust me, it’s way more impactful when you watch the scene. The blood pours over her head and face, which, according to Cardellini, required “a lot of cleanups and redos.” “That blood has to fall exactly in the right position for that stunt to work. So there were several ways we did it; for it to really have its full impact on my face, it took a few takes,” she said. Added Kane, “A lot of the gags in the show are very complicated. The special effects gags are very complicated. Linda had to go through a lot, and they’re very hard to reset. We didn’t have a lot of opportunities to do that. And I’d like to give my props right now here in front of all of you to Linda; she nailed it every single time. There was never an, ‘Oh, Linda was not in the right place.’ No, she nailed it every time. So it was a pleasure working with her on these complicated gags because she’s a consummate pro.” Jacob Elordi Circling Ari Aster’s A24 Film Starring Scarlett Johansson Cal AG Bonta Claims Ellison Misinformation, Side Deals In WBD Merger Caitríona Balfe Leads Alfonso Cuarón Horror Series ‘Ascension’ Ordered By Apple TV Second Fastest To Cross $1B WW; Now India’s Biggest Ever Hollywood Pic Read More About: Comments

title: Gramado Film Festival Launches New Talent Drive
full_text: Aug 10, 2026 11:21pm PT Gramado Film Festival Launches New Talent Drive The inaugural Residency for 60 young filmmakers will offer an intensive program running Aug. 17-19 By Marcelo Cajueiro Plus Icon Marcelo Cajueiro Latest Gramado Film Festival Hosts the First International Meeting of Cities 3 hours ago Luiz Carlos Barreto, Brazil’s Legendary Film Producer, Dies at 98 3 weeks ago Brazil’s Gramado Fest Set to Honor ‘I’m Still Here’ Star Selton Mello and ‘The Secret Agent’ Standout Maria Fernanda Cândido 3 weeks ago See All Marcio Fraccaroli, Veronica Stumpf and Silvio Guindane will headline masterclasses at the Gramado Residency Credit: Lucas Ramos, Guto Costa The first Residency for Young Filmmakers, a new feature of the Gramado Film Market taking place Aug. 17-19, will count with the participation of 60 filmmakers aged between 18 and 35, selected from more than 200 applications. Participants are required to have work experience on at least one film, mostly in the fields of production, direction, acting, screenwriting, cinematography or sound. Rio Grande do Sul, where Gramado is located, is the state with most participants: 28. The remaining come from the states of Bahia, Goiás, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Santa Catarina, Sergipe and Pernambuco, and the Federal District. Related Stories Don Lemon Asks Court to Drop Criminal Charges Against Him Related to Minnesota ICE Protest, Citing Donald Trump's Chronic 'Animus' Toward Journalist Katy Perry Slams Trump Administration for Using Song 'Firework' in Military Strikes Video: 'I Absolutely Do Not Condone It' The intensive three-day program includes a total of 17 sessions in the mornings and afternoons, and the attendance of the Gramado Film Festival ’s evening screenings. The first day features masterclasses on distribution, screenwriting and directing, covering subjects from narrative construction and creative choices to strategies for positioning films in different markets. The day’s program also includes a panel on public policies for the Brazilian audiovisual sector and an event dedicated to music scoring and sound recording. Popular on Variety Over Aug. 18-19, the focus is professional integration, production and changes in the audiovisual market, with panels on true crime, career internationalization, film societies and professional sustainability, as well as masterclasses on audiovisual production and post-production and a case study. The residency concludes with sessions on cinematography and environmental sustainability in productions. Paris Filmes ’ CEO Marcio Fraccaroli and Paris Entretenimento’s producer Veronica Stumpf will conduct the residency’s first masterclass, Distribution: Paths to Finding the Audience. São Paulo-based Paris is Brazil’s leading independent film distributor and a top producer of local pics. “The purpose of this masterclass is to show that distribution goes far beyond screening a film in movie theaters. It’s a strategic stage that begins with decisions about how the work will be positioned, understanding the target audience, developing the communication campaign and choosing the best release window,” Fraccaroli told Variety . “The idea is to share some of our experience to demonstrate how each decision can directly affect a film’s reach, cultural relevance and commercial performance.” Fraccaroli added he hopes to contribute to a conversation about the future of audiovisual distribution in a context of rapid changes in content consumption: “Understanding shifts in the market and developing increasingly intelligent distribution strategies will be essential to expand the reach of films and allow them to achieve their full potential.” Stumpf celebrated the Gramado fest’s decision to launch the residency initiative. “It is essential to discuss and encourage the training of new professionals in order to strengthen the Brazilian audiovisual sector,” she told Variety . “As it is constantly changing, the market increasingly demands knowledge, planning and strategic vision. Training filmmakers, producers and executives who are capable of understanding the entire audiovisual value chain is essential for Brazil to consolidate a stronger, more competitive industry that is prepared to engage with different audiences, both within the country and abroad.” Actor, director, producer, screenwriter and playwright Silvio Guindane will teach the masterclass Directing: Choices That Build the Film. Guindane has starred in dozens of films, telenovelas and series. He broke through as a director with the film “Mussum, o Filmis,” a biopic about comedian and musician Mussum. The feature premiered at the Gramado Film Festival in 2023, taking home awards for film, actor for Aílton Graça, supporting actress for Neusa Borges, supporting actor for Yuri Marçal, original score and the audience award. “Training new filmmakers is fundamental for the market,” Guindane told Variety . “Film is an industrial art because it involves so many people, and a film set is a big thing. But it’s also a handcrafted art. The filmmaker has the role of a conductor, which is to orchestrate talent, to manage, to draw from each department, each person in each department, including and especially the actors, the best they have to give to the characters and to the film as a whole.” ‘Sholay’ to Make ‘Films in Concert’ World Premiere at London’s Royal Albert Hall Sony’s Indian Version of ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?’ Hosted by Amitabh Bachchan, Adds Google Gemini as AI Guide (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: Heritage Monday at the Locarno Film Festival Sees a Future in the Past
full_text: Aug 10, 2026 11:12pm PT Heritage Monday at the Locarno Film Festival Sees a Future in the Past Young people are discovering black and white classics and 'feel the need to go back' to better understand how films were made, according to panelists By John Bleasdale Plus Icon John Bleasdale Guest Contributor Latest Heritage Monday at the Locarno Film Festival Sees a Future in the Past 4 hours ago Zoe Saldaña on Seeing ‘Terminator’ Aged 7, Having the Wrong-Shaped Feet and Wanting to Direct: ‘Give Me That Camera!’ 20 hours ago Protest at the Locarno Film Festival Remembers 60,000 Names of the Dead of Gaza 2 days ago See All Heritage Monday at the Locarno Film Festival Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival/Ti-Press Heritage Monday has become a popular fixture at the industry section of the Locarno Film Festival , reflecting the growing interest in film restoration and retrospective programming. This year’s edition was specifically devoted to the challenge of gaining new young audiences for older films. The panel, moderated by Sung Moon of the Jeonju International Film Festival, featured contributions from Leslie Vuchot of Timeless Cinema from France, Amy Homma from the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection in the U.S., Arsenal Filminstitut’s Stefanie Schulte Strathaus from Germany and American author and programmer Eddie Muller from the Film Noir Foundation. Related Stories Dylan Mulvaney Fires Back After Trump Mocks Her and Kaitlan Collins in White House Correspondents' Dinner Speech: 'Actually the Greatest Compliment of All' CNN's Kaitlan Collins Was 'Not Surprised' Trump Insulted Her in White House Correspondents' Dinner Speech: 'That Happens Pretty Regularly Inside the Oval Office' “When we give the chance to younger people to speak about something, it’s almost never about a recent film,” Vuchot said, citing her experience in running Le Lucernaire cinema in Paris. “It’s about something that’s been transmitted, transferred, and that they want to share as well. […] Young people feel the need to go back, even if it’s from books and stuff, to how films were made, going back to the roots and understanding where filmmakers got their inspiration from.” Popular on Variety For Muller, host of TCM’s “Noir Alley,” the key has been to replicate the mid-20th century, film-going experience, with double features and ushers as part of the atmosphere. A virtuous circle is created as the proceeds from festivals are poured into restoring films which can then be shown at festivals. His role as a host on Turner Classic Movies has also proved a turning point, increasing his visibility. He has brought school classes into his festivals and followed it up with lessons in schools and seen how students who had never seen a black and white film before on the big screen reacted to Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall in “To Have and Have Not.” Muller says: “In a class of 35 students, if you’re lucky, you’re going to connect with six that are really into it, and the other kids are using social media to ignore everything that you’re talking about. But those six are really connecting in a way that will make a difference to their lives.” Despite the ravages of TikTok, Homma argued for pragmatic optimism: “When we’re thinking of our audience, it’s so important for us to try and meet all of our audience members where they’re at, and not assume that they all understand that more cerebral motivation for why we go to a film.” One example to encourage engagement was to bring a real Dalmation — Pogo — to a screening of “101 Dalmations,” with an animator leading live-drawing classes and talking about the techniques used in the film. They also invited Guillermo del Toro to the museum and use the archive to illustrate his talk on films by Alfred Hitchcock. As well as repertory cinemas such as the Academy and Le Lucernaire presenting films, heritage is also proving popular in general distribution. “There’s an urgent need that comes really from the present,” Schulte Strathaus believes. “Heritage film offers so many potential futures, and in a time where we don’t see a future anymore or it’s hard to see a future, we go back into film history, and see all those told and untold and ignored narratives, all those could have beens like those other potential histories that we didn’t know about or that didn’t make it into the present, and that maybe could have led us into a better present.” Some problems were identified, such as the perennial need to secure funding whether from private donors or larger organizations or in a more grassroots way. Likewise, securing and even identifying rights continues to be a problem, which can even extend to subtitles, which might be copyrighted and need to be duplicated, causing unnecessary expenses. The solution proposed was more cooperation and coordination between archives, cinematheques and organizations internationally. Climate controlled archives are closing and even an internationally famous body such as the Motion Picture Academy is being overwhelmed by a growing amount of material while operating with the same number of staff and financial resources. “I’m a forever optimist,” Homma says. “We are seeing more people care about the films.” For Schulte Strathaus, who specializes in avant-garde film, the solution is to build communities who are not just audiences but who can creatively participate in the restorations, either for educational purposes or as artists helping in the preservation of filmmakers’ work. ‘Sholay’ to Make ‘Films in Concert’ World Premiere at London’s Royal Albert Hall Sony’s Indian Version of ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?’ Hosted by Amitabh Bachchan, Adds Google Gemini as AI Guide (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: European Broadcast Giant RTL Group Bets on Streaming to Fuel Growth
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All August 10, 2026 11:00pm RTL Group CEO Clement Schwebig Boris-Breuer RTL Group , Europe’s largest television conglomerate, is going full in on streaming. First half figures at RTL, released Tuesday, showed sharp growth in revenues — up 27.2 percent to was up 27.2 per cent to $345 million (€299 million) — in the company’s streaming platforms, including RTL+ in Germany and M6+ in France. The boost made up for declines in RTL’s traditional TV business, where TV advertising revenue fell 4 percent and its production operations, at subsidiary Fremantle , were down 7.7 percent year on year at $964 million (€835 million). (RTL said business at Fremantle would pick up by year end with the roll out of new productions, including its Baywatch reboot ). Related Stories Movies James Gray Rejects Men Not Being "Allowed to Engage With the Tender Side" Movies Keke Palmer, Deepa Mehta, Jacob Tremblay, and Jeremy Irons Projects Set for TIFF Financing Market “Our streaming businesses deliver strong profitability,” said RTL Group CEO Clément Schwebig in a statement. “Sreaming revenue and paid subscriptions continue to grow dynamically. As a result, streaming is now expected to contribute around €100 million ($115 million) to our full-year operating profit.” RTL’s results are the first since it’s acquisition of pay-TV group Sky Deutschland from Comcast closed June 1. The deal will see Sky Deutschland merge with RTL+, creating a streaming operating with 12.4 million paid subscriptions across Germany, Austria and Switzerland, “We are now the clear number three in the German-speaking streaming market,” said Schwebig, who called the Sky Deutschland deal “transformational” for RTL. “We confirm our target to deliver € 250 million ($289 million) in annual synergies within three years. Our transformation strategy is delivering tangible results, and we are executing it with speed and discipline. Including the effects from the Sky Deutschland acquisition, we expect to grow to between €7.1 billion and €7.2 billion ($8.2 billion – $8.3 billion) in full-year revenue with an adjusted EBITA of €725 million ($837 million).” RTL’s Sky Deutschland acquisition is part of a broader wave of consolidation across the European broadcasting market. Last month, Comcast‘s Sky in the U.K. inked a $2.13 billion (£1.6 billion) deal to acquire the media and entertainment (M&E) unit of commercial broadcast giant ITV. Last year, MediaForEurope (MFE), the TV group controlled by the Berlusconi family, took majority control of ProSiebenSat.1, Germany’s number two commercial TV group, adding to MFE’s European network stable, that already includes Italy’s largest broadcaster, Mediaset, and Spain’s No. 1 commercial network Telecinco. The merger mania is on the production side too. On July 9, French production giant Banijay, producers of Peaky Blinders , Big Brother , and MasterChef , joined up with and U.K. production powerhouse All3Media ( The Traitors , Squid Game: The Challenge ) in a deal with an enterprise value of $8 billion. French broadcaster TF1 has reportedly put its production and distribution arm, Studio TF1, on the market. A sale the division, formerly known as Newen Studios, could fetch up to $450 million. And ITV Studios, producers of Love Island and I’m a Celebrity…Get Me Out of Here! , newly independent in the wake of ITV network’s sale to Sky, could also be a takeover target, as well as a potential buyer. All across Europe, the television industry is scrambling to get big quick to avoid dying at the hands of competition from YouTube and the global streaming giants. THR

title: ‘Sunset P.I.’ Bosses Dan Goor & Luke Del Tredici On Finding Inspiration From ‘Moonlighting’ & ‘The Pitt’

They were joined by series stars Jake Johnson, Keith David, Langston Kerman, and Mary Shalaby, Sunset P.I. is a half-hour comedy that centers on Mickey (Johnson), who is smart, cynical, and heartbroken, but trying to pretend he’s not. Mickey is a private investigator with a knack for solving cases and a former LAPD cop whose life imploded three years ago. David plays Mickey’s boss, Garner Taggart, who runs the Garner Taggart PI Agency where his son Mitch (Kerman) and Mickey are the main PIs. Shalaby plays Raya, who also works at the PI Agency.
